questions.question: What does 'deterministic polynomial-time primality test' mean?
options: Algorithm outputs prime/composite with 100% certainty in time polynomial in log n
Algorithm outputs the smallest prime factor of n using random oracle access
Algorithm needs exponential time but never errs on prime / composite inputs
Algorithm runs in O(log n) time and answers correctly only with high probability
questions.explanation: Deterministic + polynomial-time in log n + always correct. AKS (2002) was the first.

questions.question: Before AKS, what was the status of deterministic primality testing?
options: Best deterministic test was conditional on Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (Miller)
Best test was sub-exponential and unconditional via the Quadratic Sieve method
All deterministic tests were exponential; no polynomial algorithm existed
Miller-Rabin was already deterministic when checking enough fixed-base witnesses
questions.explanation: Pre-2002: Miller's deterministic test was poly-time but assumed GRH. APR test was sub-exponential. AKS gave the first unconditional polynomial deterministic test.

questions.question: AKS is based on which identity?
options: (X + a)^n ≡ X^n + a (mod n, X^r − 1) iff n is prime (for suitable r, a)
n^(n−1) ≡ 1 (mod n) for every coprime base, iff n is prime (Fermat-style)
Σ_{k=1}^{n} k^(n−1) ≡ −1 (mod n) iff n is a prime by Wilson generalization
Π_{a=1}^{n−1} (X − a) ≡ X^(n−1) − 1 (mod n) iff n is prime (Lagrange)
questions.explanation: AKS core identity: for n > 1 and gcd(a, n) = 1, (X+a)^n ≡ X^n + a (mod n) in Z[X]/(X^r − 1) iff n is prime (for suitable r and enough a's).

questions.question: What is the runtime of the original AKS algorithm in `b = log n` bits?
options: O(b^12) — later improved to Õ(b^6) by Lenstra-Pomerance and other refinements
O(b^2) — same as schoolbook multiplication of two n-bit integers exactly
O(b) — linear in the bit length but with massive hidden constants in practice
O(2^b) — exponential because AKS sweeps every possible witness base a
questions.explanation: Original AKS: Õ(b^12). Lenstra-Pomerance variant: Õ(b^6). Polynomial, but vastly slower than Miller-Rabin in practice.

questions.question: Why is AKS rarely used in production cryptography?
options: Constant factors dwarf Miller-Rabin; MR's 4^{−k} error suffices for keygen
AKS only works for primes of special form like Mersenne or Fermat primes
AKS leaks the bit-length of n via timing channels in its polynomial loop
AKS depends on the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, like the Miller test
questions.explanation: Miller-Rabin with 40+ rounds gives error < 2^−80 in milliseconds. AKS takes minutes-to-hours on cryptographic-sized n. Theoretically beautiful, practically dominated by MR + ECPP for certification.

questions.question: What does ECPP (Elliptic Curve Primality Proving) give that AKS does not?
options: A short verifiable certificate of primality that anyone can recheck quickly
A faster deterministic test running in O(log² n) time without GRH assumptions
A randomized test with provable success probability above 99.99% per attempt
A test that works for composite n by returning the smallest non-trivial factor
questions.explanation: ECPP produces a primality certificate (Atkin-Morain). Verifying is O(log⁴ n); generating is heuristically Õ(log⁴ n). Used to certify primes in databases.

questions.question: The choice of `r` in AKS satisfies: order of n modulo r is greater than what?
options: log² n — the threshold from the AKS theorem that guarantees correctness
log n — sufficient for the simpler Fouvry-style variants but not full AKS
√n — chosen to balance the size of the polynomial ring against trial division
n^(1/3) — picked to minimize total work across the AKS verification loop
questions.explanation: AKS picks smallest r with ord_r(n) > log² n. Such r exists with r = O(log⁵ n) (Fouvry's theorem).

questions.question: An attacker tricks a verifier into accepting a composite `n` as prime using which strategy?
options: Submit a forged ECPP-style certificate referencing a non-existent prime factor
Exploit Miller-Rabin liars for n by choosing bases that happen to be silent witnesses
Run AKS on a known Carmichael composite knowing the test will misclassify it
Trick the verifier into trial-dividing only by primes that miss n's small factors
questions.explanation: Forged certificates: if the verifier doesn't recursively check each prime factor cited, attacker can lie. Real primality proofs (ECPP, Pratt) are self-verifying — every cited prime gets its own certificate.
